claim: 92–94% of the human genome is subject to alternative splicing
source: Pre-mRNA splicing plays a key role in global regulation of the transcriptome and thus the proteome, with 92–94% of the human genome subject to alternative splicing (Wang et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2008

claim: >80% of alternative splicing is predicted to impact protein functionality
source: >80% of alternative splicing predicted to impact protein functionality (Yura et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yura et al., 2006

claim: SRSF1 limits autoimmunity via a role in maintaining healthy regulatory T cells
source: SRSF1, the best studied SR protein, limits autoimmunity via a role in maintaining healthy regulatory T cells (Katsuyama and Moulton, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Katsuyama and Moulton, 2021

claim: SRSF3 negatively regulates IL-1β release during Escherichia coli infection of THP-1 monocytes
source: SRSF3 has been shown to negatively regulate IL-1β release during Escherichia coli infection of THP-1 monocytes (Moura-Alves et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moura-Alves et al., 2011

claim: SRSF2 promotes herpes simplex virus replication by binding to viral promoters and controlling splicing of viral transcripts
source: SRSF2 promotes herpes simplex virus replication by binding to viral promoters and controlling splicing of viral transcripts (Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: SRSF6 is a 55 kDa protein
source: SRSF6 is a 55 kDa protein that is essential for viability of Drosophilia melanogaster and Mus musculus (Mason et al., 2020; Ring and Lis, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mason et al., 2020 and Ring and Lis, 1994

claim: SRSF6 is essential for viability of Drosophilia melanogaster and Mus musculus
source: SRSF6 is a 55 kDa protein that is essential for viability of Drosophilia melanogaster and Mus musculus (Mason et al., 2020; Ring and Lis, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mason et al., 2020 and Ring and Lis, 1994

claim: SRSF6 preferentially binds purine-rich exonic splicing enhancers with a predicted consensus site in humans of USCGKM
source: Multiple studies report that SRSF6 preferentially binds purine-rich exonic splicing enhancers, with a predicted consensus site in humans of USCGKM (where S represents G or C; K represents U or G; M represents A or C) (Liu et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 1998

claim: SRSF6 activity is controlled via phosphorylation by the dual specificity kinases CLK1 and DYRK1a
source: SRSF6 activity is at least in part controlled via phosphorylation by the dual specificity kinases CLK1 and DYRK1a (Hara et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hara et al., 2013 and Yin et al., 2012

claim: Phosphorylation activates SRSF6 shuttling between the cytoplasm and the nucleus
source: SRSF6 activity is at least in part controlled via phosphorylation by the dual specificity kinases CLK1 and DYRK1a (Hara et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2012), which activates SRSF6 shuttling between the cytoplasm and the nucleus (Sapra et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sapra et al., 2009

claim: Loss of SRSF6 decreases mitochondrial respiration in human endoC-BH1 endothelial cells
source: For example, loss of SRSF6 decreases mitochondrial respiration, leading to increased cellular apoptosis in human endoC-BH1 endothelial cells, likely via alternative splicing of cell death factors like Bim, Bax, Diablo, and Bclaf1 (Juan-Mateu et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Juan-Mateu et al., 2018

claim: Loss of SRSF6 leads to increased cellular apoptosis in human endoC-BH1 endothelial cells
source: For example, loss of SRSF6 decreases mitochondrial respiration, leading to increased cellular apoptosis in human endoC-BH1 endothelial cells, likely via alternative splicing of cell death factors like Bim, Bax, Diablo, and Bclaf1 (Juan-Mateu et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Juan-Mateu et al., 2018

claim: Phosphorylation of SRSF6 induces alternative splicing of mitochondria related genes in a mouse model of fatty liver disease
source: Likewise, phosphorylation of SRSF6 induces alternative splicing of mitochondria related genes (e.g. Polg2, Nudt13, Guf1, RnaseI, and Nme4) in a mouse model of fatty liver disease as well as in human hepatitis patients (Li et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2021

claim: Phosphorylation of SRSF6 induces alternative splicing of mitochondria related genes in human hepatitis patients
source: Likewise, phosphorylation of SRSF6 induces alternative splicing of mitochondria related genes (e.g. Polg2, Nudt13, Guf1, RnaseI, and Nme4) in a mouse model of fatty liver disease as well as in human hepatitis patients (Li et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2021

claim: SRSF6 is unique amongst the SR proteins queried based on hierarchical clustering of gene expression profiles
source: Using a simple hierarchical clustering algorithm, we visualized the gene expression profiles of each SR KD macrophage cell line and pinpointed SRSF6 as unique amongst the SR proteins queried (correlation between SRSF6's node and the rest of the tree = 0.138) (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and visualization in Figure 1A showing correlation value of 0.138

claim: Loss of SRSF6 results in downregulation of genes related to mitochondrial biology
source: Manual annotation of genes in clusters that were uniquely impacted by loss of SRSF6 revealed several downregulated genes related to mitochondrial biology (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and visualization in Figure 1B

claim: Loss of SRSF6 results in upregulation of interferon stimulated genes
source: On the other hand, many upregulated genes fell into the category of interferon stimulated genes (ISGs) (Figure 1C), as defined by Kim et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2006; Zahoor et al., 2014
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data, visualization in Figure 1C, and citations defining ISGs

claim: Elevated reads across all coding exons for Rsad2 are observed in Srsf6 KD cells
source: Direct visualization of RNA-seq reads using the Integrated Genome Viewer shows elevated reads across all coding exons for representative ISGs Rsad2 (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by IGV visualization in Figure 1D

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis confirmed overrepresentation of differentially expressed genes in functional categories related to interferon and antiviral responses in Srsf6 KD cells
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis confirmed overrepresentation of differentially expressed genes in functional categories related to interferon and antiviral responses (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis results shown in Figure 1E

claim: The degree of ISG accumulation correlates with SRSF6 KD efficiency and protein expression
source: Furthermore, RT-qPCR confirmed basal ISG expression in two independently derived Srsf6 KD cell lines (Figure 1H–J), with the degree of ISG accumulation correlating with SRSF6 KD efficiency and protein expression (Figure 1F–G)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data in Figures 1F-J

claim: Transient siRNA KD of SRSF6 in RAW MΦ cells results in ISG accumulation
source: We also measured ISG accumulation upon transient siRNA KD of SRSF6 in RAW MΦ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), arguing against off-target effects resulting from stable selection of KD cell lines
evidence: Supported by siRNA KD data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Srsf6 siRNA KD in primary bone marrow derived macrophages results in ISG accumulation
source: Importantly, this phenotype was recapitulated by Srsf6 siRNA KD in primary cell types including bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) (Figure 1K)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in BMDMs shown in Figure 1K

claim: Srsf6 siRNA KD in mouse embryonic fibroblasts results in ISG accumulation
source: Importantly, this phenotype was recapitulated by Srsf6 siRNA KD in primary cell types including bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) (Figure 1K) and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in MEFs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Differential expression of genes involved in type I IFN responses was not observed in other resting SRSF KD RAW MΦ cell lines
source: Differential expression of genes involved in type I IFN responses was not observed in other resting SRSF KD RAW MΦ cell lines, suggesting this phenotype is unique to loss of SRSF6 and is not a general consequence of interfering with splicing (Wagner et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by comparison with other SRSF KD cell lines and citation to Wagner et al., 2021

claim: Resting Srsf6 KD macrophages have increased levels of phospho-IRF3 (S396)
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed increased levels of phospho-IRF3 (S396) in resting Srsf6 KD macrophages (Figure 1L)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1L

claim: Higher levels of IFN-β protein are measured in the supernatants of Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells
source: Higher levels of IFN-β protein were also measured in the supernatants of Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells via ISRE reporter cells (Hoffpauir et al., 2020; Figure 1M)
evidence: Supported by ISRE reporter assay data in Figure 1M and citation to Hoffpauir et al., 2020

claim: Supernatants from Srsf6 KD macrophages are sufficient to stimulate ISG expression in naïve wild-type RAW MΦ cells
source: Consistent with higher levels of IFN-β secretion, supernatants from Srsf6 KD macrophages were sufficient to stimulate ISG expression in naïve wild-type RAW MΦ cells (24 hr incubation) (Figure 1N)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1N

claim: Elevated basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD cells is rescued by treatment with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody
source: Elevated basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD cells was rescued by treatment with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody (Figure 1O)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with antibody treatment in Figure 1O

claim: IRF3-mediated expression of IFN-β drives upregulation of basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells
source: Together, these data suggest that IRF3-mediated expression of IFN-β drives upregulation of basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including phospho-IRF3 levels, IFN-β secretion, and antibody neutralization

claim: VSV replication is dramatically restricted in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells compared with SCR controls
source: We observed a dramatic restriction of VSV replication in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells compared with SCR controls (Figure 1P and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data of VSV replication in Figures 1P and 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: SRSF6 is a negative regulator of antiviral immunity
source: We observed a dramatic restriction of VSV replication in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells compared with SCR controls (Figure 1P and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), supporting a bona fide role for SRSF6 as a negative regulator of antiviral immunity
evidence: Inferred from VSV restriction data and overall ISG phenotype

claim: Mitochondrial DNA can activate cytosolic DNA sensing pathways when mitochondria are damaged or depolarized
source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can activate cytosolic DNA sensing pathways when mitochondria are damaged or depolarized such that mtDNA is released from the inner matrix (West et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to West et al., 2015

claim: Cytosolic mtDNA is significantly enriched in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells
source: We detected significant enrichment of several mtDNA genes (Cytb, Dloop2, and Dloop1) in the cytosol of Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data of cytosolic fractions in Figure 2B

claim: mtDNA depletion via treatment with ddC returns expression of Rsad2 to that of SCR control cells in Srsf6 KD macrophages
source: Additionally, we determined the necessity of mtDNA to drive the increased basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD macrophages, as mtDNA depletion via treatment with the nucleoside analog 2,3'-dideoxycytidine (ddC) (Figure 2C), returned expression of the ISG Rsad2 to that of SCR control cells (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with ddC treatment in Figures 2C and 2D

claim: Elevated basal ISG expression in Srsf6 KD cells is dependent on the cytosolic DNA sensor cGAS
source: Elevated basal ISG expression was dependent on cytosolic DNA sensing, as Srsf6 KD did not cause Rsad2 transcript accumulation in the absence of the cytosolic DNA sensor, cGAS (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in cGAS KO cells in Figures 2E-F and 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Loss of SRSF6 causes leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol where it engages cGAS, leading to phosphorylation of IRF3, expression of IFN-β, and activation of ISG expression
source: Together, these data argue that loss of SRSF6 causes leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol where it engages cGAS, leading to phosphorylation of IRF3 (Figure 1L), expression of IFN-β (Figure 1M), and activation of ISG expression in resting macrophages (Figure 1A–C)
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including cytosolic mtDNA enrichment, cGAS dependency, and IFN-β signaling

claim: Srsf6 KD MEFs exhibit increased mitochondrial fragmentation
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy (anti-TOM20) revealed increased mitochondrial fragmentation in Srsf6 KD MEFs (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2G

claim: Total levels of mitochondrial proteins TOM20 and VDAC are comparable between SCR and Srsf6 KD cell lines
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy (anti-TOM20) revealed increased mitochondrial fragmentation in Srsf6 KD MEFs (Figure 2G), although total levels of mitochondrial proteins like TOM20 and VDAC were comparable between SCR and Srsf6 KD cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Mitochondria in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ exhibit loss of membrane potential
source: Importantly, mitochondria in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ also exhibited loss of membrane potential (Figure 2H), as measured by tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE) signal (decreased TMRE signal = increased membrane depolarization)
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data in Figure 2H

claim: Loss of SRSF6 reduces mitochondrial OXPHOS, indicated by lower basal and maximal respiration
source: Srsf6 KD cells displayed deficiencies in multiple readouts of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), which serves as a proxy for oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Loss of SRSF6 reduced mitochondrial OXPHOS, indicated by lower basal and maximal respiration
evidence: Supported by Seahorse metabolic analysis data in Figures 2I and 2J

claim: Srsf6 KD mitochondria have lower ATP production and lower respiratory capacity compared with SCR controls
source: Additionally, Srsf6 KD mitochondria had lower ATP production and lower respiratory capacity compared with SCR controls (Figure 2I top-J)
evidence: Supported by Seahorse metabolic analysis data in Figures 2I and 2J

claim: Glycolysis is unaffected by SRSF6 knockdown
source: Glycolysis, as measured by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was unaffected by SRSF6 knockdown (Figure 2I, bottom)
evidence: Supported by Seahorse ECAR data in Figure 2I

claim: SRSF6 specifically impacts cellular metabolism primarily at the level of mitochondrial OXPHOS
source: Glycolysis, as measured by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was unaffected by SRSF6 knockdown (Figure 2I, bottom), suggesting that SRSF6 specifically impacts cellular metabolism primarily at the level of mitochondrial OXPHOS
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on OXPHOS vs. glycolysis

claim: SRSF6 mostly controls exon inclusion in macrophages with 1043 exon skipping LSVs
source: As expected for an SR protein, SRSF6 mostly controls exon inclusion in macrophages (1043 exon skipping LSVs), with changes in intron retention (247 LSVs), and alternative 5' (206 LSVs) and 3' (233 LSVs) splice site usage also detected (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by MAJIQ analysis data shown in Figure 3A

claim: SRSF6-dependent splicing of intron 2 in the Xaf1 pre-mRNA is predicted to introduce a premature stop codon and target Xaf1 for nonsense mediated decay
source: Semi-quantitative RT-PCR was used to validate hits and SRSF6-dependent splicing of intron 2 in the Xaf1 pre-mRNA, which is predicted to introduce a premature stop codon and target Xaf1 for nonsense mediated decay, was confirmed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and prediction of premature stop codon

claim: MAJIQ analysis measured preferential retention of intron 1 in Bax in Srsf6 KD macrophages
source: One alternative splicing event with unique protein coding capacity that piqued our interest occurred in Bax, the mitochondrial pore-forming protein and executioner of apoptosis. Specifically, MAJIQ analysis measured preferential retention of intron 1 in Srsf6 KD macrophages (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by MAJIQ analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Considerable Bax intron 1 retention occurs in SCR MΦ cells but to a lesser extent than in Srsf6 KD cells
source: Considerable Bax intron 1 retention occurred in SCR MΦ cells as well, but to a lesser extent (Figure 3C–E)
evidence: Supported by MAJIQ analysis and IGV data in Figures 3C-E

claim: SRSF6-dependent Bax splicing was validated by RT-qPCR
source: We validated SRSF6-dependent Bax splicing by RT-qPCR, using a forward primer in exon 1 and a reverse primer in intron 1 (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3F

claim: SRSF6-dependent Bax splicing was validated by semi-quantitative RT-PCR
source: We validated SRSF6-dependent Bax splicing by RT-qPCR, using a forward primer in exon 1 and a reverse primer in intron 1 (Figure 3F), as well as by semi-quantitative RT-PCR, using a forward primer in exon 1 and a reverse primer in exon 6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Increased Bax alternative splicing does not impact total BAX protein expression
source: Increased Bax alternative splicing did not impact total BAX protein expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Retention of intron 1 in Bax causes usage of a downstream ATG start site encoded in exon 2, creating a 20 amino acid N-terminal truncation
source: Retention of intron 1 in Bax causes usage of a downstream ATG start site encoded in exon 2, which creates a 20 amino acid N-terminal truncation, but otherwise leaves the Bax coding sequence completely in-frame and intact (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figures 3G and 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: BAX-κ is upregulated in the rat hippocampus following cerebral ischemic injury
source: This annotated isoform of BAX, dubbed BAX kappa (BAX-κ; GenBank accession number AY095934), is upregulated in the rat hippocampus following cerebral ischemic injury and promotes apoptosis when overexpressed in murine hippocampal neuronal cells (Jin et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jin et al., 2001

claim: BAX-κ promotes apoptosis when overexpressed in murine hippocampal neuronal cells
source: This annotated isoform of BAX, dubbed BAX kappa (BAX-κ; GenBank accession number AY095934), is upregulated in the rat hippocampus following cerebral ischemic injury and promotes apoptosis when overexpressed in murine hippocampal neuronal cells (Jin et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jin et al., 2001

claim: Bax-κ is predicted to be functionally analogous to the human BAX-psi isoform
source: Because they both lack an ART (apoptosis-regulating targeting) sequence (Cartron et al., 2005; Goping et al., 1998), Bax-κ is predicted to be functionally analogous to the human BAX-psi isoform, which has been shown to constitutively associate with mitochondria (Cartron et al., 2005)
evidence: Inferred from shared lack of ART sequence and citation to Cartron et al., 2005

claim: Human BAX-psi has been shown to constitutively associate with mitochondria
source: Because they both lack an ART (apoptosis-regulating targeting) sequence (Cartron et al., 2005; Goping et al., 1998), Bax-κ is predicted to be functionally analogous to the human BAX-psi isoform, which has been shown to constitutively associate with mitochondria (Cartron et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cartron et al., 2005

claim: ESE Finder identified three strong SRSF6 consensus sequences in Bax exons 1, 3, and 6
source: ESE Finder, a web-based platform to identify exonic splicing enhancer motifs (Cartegni et al., 2003), identified three strong SRSF6 consensus sequences in Bax exons 1, 3, and 6 (Figure 3H)
evidence: Supported by ESE Finder analysis shown in Figure 3H and citation to Cartegni et al., 2003

claim: CLIP experiments show clear enrichment of Bax transcripts bound to 3xFLAG-SRSF6 compared with a 3xFLAG-GFP control
source: UV Crosslinking-immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments in RAW MΦ cells showed a clear enrichment of Bax transcripts bound to 3xFLAG-SRSF6 compared with a 3xFLAG-GFP control (Figure 3I–J)
evidence: Supported by CLIP-qPCR data in Figures 3I-J

claim: SRSF6 controls splicing of Bax intron 1 by directly binding consensus exonic splicing enhancers in Bax exons
source: Together, these data strongly suggest that SRSF6 controls splicing of Bax intron 1 by directly binding consensus exonic splicing enhancers in Bax exons
evidence: Inferred from ESE Finder predictions and CLIP experimental results

claim: BAX pores can release mtDNA capable of stimulating cGAS-dependent type I IFN responses
source: Previous literature has demonstrated that in addition to promoting release of cytochrome c during apoptosis, BAX pores can release mtDNA capable of stimulating cGAS-dependent type I IFN responses (Rongvaux, 2018; Rongvaux et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rongvaux, 2018 and Rongvaux et al., 2014

claim: Modest knockdown of Bax via siRNA transfection rescues high Rsad2 and Ifit1 expression in Srsf6 KD macrophages
source: Consistent with this prediction, even modest knockdown of Bax (all isoforms) via siRNA transfection rescued high Rsad2 and Ifit1 expression in Srsf6 KD macrophages (Figure 3K)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with Bax siRNA in Figure 3K

claim: Knockdown of Bax in wild-type RAW MΦ has no impact on Rsad2 or Isg15 expression
source: Because knockdown of Bax in wild-type RAW MΦ had no impact on Rsad2 or Isg15 expression (Figure 3L), we can conclude that links between aberrant basal ISG expression and BAX are limited to Srsf6 KD cells in which Bax splicing is defective
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3L

claim: Links between aberrant basal ISG expression and BAX are limited to Srsf6 KD cells in which Bax splicing is defective
source: Because knockdown of Bax in wild-type RAW MΦ had no impact on Rsad2 or Isg15 expression (Figure 3L), we can conclude that links between aberrant basal ISG expression and BAX are limited to Srsf6 KD cells in which Bax splicing is defective
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of Bax KD in SCR vs. Srsf6 KD cells

claim: Significantly higher levels of PI incorporation are observed in Srsf6 KD cell lines compared to SCR controls
source: We observed significantly higher levels of PI incorporation in Srsf6 KD cell lines (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by PI incorporation data in Figure 4A

claim: A population of stable Srsf6 KD MΦ undergoes cell death even in the absence of cell death inducing agents
source: We observed significantly higher levels of PI incorporation in Srsf6 KD cell lines (Figure 4A), suggesting that even in the absence of cell death inducing agents, a population of stable Srsf6 KD MΦ undergoes cell death
evidence: Inferred from PI incorporation data in resting cells

claim: Treatment with anti-IFN-β neutralizing antibody has no effect on PI incorporation in SCR or Srsf6 KD cells
source: Treatment with an anti-IFN-β neutralizing antibody had no effect on PI incorporation in SCR or Srsf6 KD cells, effectively ruling out a role for IFN−β in mediating SRSF6-dependent cell death (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by PI incorporation data with antibody treatment in Figure 4B

claim: IFN-β does not mediate SRSF6-dependent cell death
source: Treatment with an anti-IFN-β neutralizing antibody had no effect on PI incorporation in SCR or Srsf6 KD cells, effectively ruling out a role for IFN−β in mediating SRSF6-dependent cell death (Figure 4B)
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of IFN-β neutralizing antibody on cell death

claim: Flow cytometric analysis confirms higher levels of PI incorporation in Srsf6 KD cells
source: Flow cytometric analysis of Srsf6 KD cells via PI and annexin V staining (a protein that preferentially binds to phosphatidylserine on cells undergoing apoptosis), confirmed higher levels of PI incorporation in the absence of Srsf6 (Figure 4C–D)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 4C-D

claim: A population of pro-apoptotic cells (annexin V-positive but PI-negative) is more abundant in Srsf6 KDs
source: It also identified a population of pro-apoptotic cells (annexin V-positive but PI-negative) that is more abundant in Srsf6 KDs (6.3% in KD1 and 9.7% in KD2 vs. 4.2% in SCR) (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E

claim: Significantly more Srsf6 KD cells stain PI+ after treatment with low levels of staurosporine
source: Consistent with Srsf6 KD RAW 264.7 cells being prone to apoptosis, significantly more Srsf6 cells stained PI +after treatment with low levels of the apoptosis-inducing drugs staurosporine (Figure 4F)
evidence: Supported by PI incorporation data with staurosporine treatment in Figure 4F

claim: Significantly more Srsf6 KD cells stain PI+ after treatment with ABT373
source: Consistent with Srsf6 KD RAW 264.7 cells being prone to apoptosis, significantly more Srsf6 cells stained PI +after treatment with low levels of the apoptosis-inducing drugs staurosporine (Figure 4F) or ABT373 (Figure 4G)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data with ABT373 treatment in Figure 4G

claim: Srsf6 KD cells show increased cell death at early time-points following treatment with etoposide
source: Consistent with Srsf6 KD RAW 264.7 cells being prone to apoptosis, significantly more Srsf6 cells stained PI +after treatment with low levels of the apoptosis-inducing drugs staurosporine (Figure 4F) or ABT373 (Figure 4G) and at early time-points following treatment with the cell death agonist etoposide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data with etoposide treatment in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: No significant difference in IL-1β release is detected between BMDMs transfected with non-targeting siRNA vs. Srsf6-targeting siRNA
source: We detected no significant difference in IL-1β release between BMDMs transfected with a non-targeting siRNA vs. Srsf6-targeting siRNA in either unprimed or poly dA:dT primed cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C)
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figures 4—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: Cell death in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells is caspase-independent
source: Curiously, despite displaying an apoptotic signature (Figure 4C, E), cell death in Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells was caspase-independent, as treatment with the pan-caspase inhibitors Q-VD-OPh (Figure 4H) and Z-VAD-FMK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) had no impact on PI incorporation in resting Srsf6 KD cells
evidence: Supported by PI incorporation data with caspase inhibitor treatment in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Resting Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ do not release cytochrome c
source: Consistent with lack of caspase involvement, resting Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ did not release cytochrome c (Figure 4I)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data of cytochrome c in cytoplasmic fractions in Figure 4I

claim: A form of mitochondrial-dependent caspase-independent cell death occurs preferentially in Srsf6 KD macrophages
source: These observations, coupled with the disruption to mitochondrial membrane potential reported in (Figure 2H), suggest a form of mitochondrial-dependent caspase-independent cell death (CICD) (as described by Xiang et al., 1996, reviewed in Tait and Green, 2008) that occurs preferentially in Srsf6 KD macrophages
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including caspase-independence, lack of cytochrome c release, and mitochondrial depolarization, with citations to Xiang et al., 1996 and Tait and Green, 2008

claim: BAX-κ can trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and release of mtDNA without releasing cytochrome c
source: We hypothesize that BAX-κ, which can trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and release of mtDNA without releasing cytochrome c, is a major contributor to this noncanonical form of cell death, which is characterized by low-level sustained damage to mitochondria
evidence: Hypothesized based on experimental observations of mtDNA release without cytochrome c release

claim: A significant increase of BAX protein on mitochondria is observed in resting Srsf6 KD cells compared with SCR controls
source: We observed a significant increase of BAX protein on mitochondria isolated from resting Srsf6 KD cells compared with SCR controls (Figure 4J bottom)
evidence: Supported by mitoFLOW data in Figure 4J

claim: Bax-κ transcripts are considerably higher in Srsf6 KD cells with low membrane potential compared with mitochondria with high membrane potential or total mitochondria
source: Bax-κ transcripts were considerably higher in Srsf6 KD cells with low membrane potential compared with mitochondria with high membrane potential or total mitochondria (Figure 4K)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from sorted cells in Figure 4K

claim: Bax-κ expression correlates with mitochondrial depolarization in SCR cells
source: Bax-κ transcripts were most abundant in low membrane potential mitochondria isolated from Srsf6 KD cells, although notably, Bax-κ expression correlated with mitochondrial depolarization in SCR cells as well
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from sorted cells

claim: Expression of BAX-κ is sufficient to induce robust basal ISG expression in wild-type RAW doxycycline-inducible cell line
source: We found that expression of BAX-κ was sufficient to induce robust basal ISG expression in the wild-type RAW doxycycline-inducible cell line (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from BAX-κ overexpression in Figure 5B

claim: ISG induction by BAX-κ is dose-dependent and seen even at early timepoints post-DOX treatment when BAX-κ ectopic expression is still quite low
source: Importantly, this ISG induction was dose-dependent and seen even at early timepoints post-DOX treatment when BAX-κ ectopic expression is still quite low (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: BAX-κ expression is sufficient to induce apoptosis and cell death at 15 h post-doxycycline treatment
source: BAX-κ expression was also sufficient to induce apoptosis and cell death, as measured by flow cytometry of PI and annexin V-stained cells at 15 h post-doxycycline treatment (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5C

claim: The accumulation of PI+ and annexin V+ cells is dependent on the dose of BAX-κ
source: The accumulation of PI + and annexin V + cells was dependent on the dose of BAX-κ
evidence: Inferred from dose-dependent effects shown in multiple figures

claim: BAX-κ induced apoptosis and cell death at 15 hr post-DOX treatment is largely caspase-dependent
source: Unlike the cell death we measured in resting Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells, BAX-κ induced apoptosis and cell death at 15 hr (Figure 5C) or 24 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) post-DOX treatment was largely caspase-dependent (Figure 5C, bottom graphs)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data with caspase inhibitor treatment in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: High levels of BAX-κ induce a level of MOMP sufficient to release cytochrome c and activate downstream caspases
source: We predict that high levels of BAX-κ in these overexpression cell lines at later time points induces a level of MOMP that is sufficient to release cytochrome c and activate downstream caspases
evidence: Predicted based on dose-dependent and time-dependent effects of BAX-κ on caspase-dependent cell death

claim: An activation signal is required for full length BAX to stimulate cell death
source: When we directly stimulated apoptosis in these cells via low levels of staurosporine (1 μM), BAX and BAX-κ expression induced similar amounts of enhanced cell death relative to GFP or BAXG179P-expressing cells, confirming that an activation signal is required for full length BAX to stimulate cell death (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by cell death data with staurosporine treatment in Figure 5E

claim: Significantly more mitochondria-associated BAX is measured in BAX-κ expressing cells compared with cells expressing BAXG179P or BAX
source: Using mitoFLOW (as in Figure 4J), we measured significantly more mitochondria-associated BAX in BAX-κ expressing cells compared with cells expressing BAXG179P or BAX (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by mitoFLOW data in Figure 5F

claim: Expression of BAX-κ is sufficient to drive ISG expression and cell death in resting macrophages
source: Collectively, these data argue that expression of BAX-κ is sufficient to drive ISG expression and cell death in resting macrophages and support a major role for BAX-κ in inducing the mitochondrial phenotypes we uncovered in Srsf6 KD macrophages
evidence: Inferred from multiple BAX-κ overexpression experiments

claim: SR proteins, including SRSF6, are differentially phosphorylated in BMDMs over a 24 hr time course of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis
source: Our original interest in SR protein function in macrophages was borne out of a global phosphoproteomics analysis that reported SR proteins, including SRSF6, were differentially phosphorylated in BMDMs at several sites over a 24 hr time course of infection with the intracellular bacterial pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) (Budzik et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Budzik et al., 2020

claim: No major differences in SRSF6 protein localization are observed in phosphomutant/mimetic cell lines compared with wild-type SRSF6
source: We observed no major differences in SRSF6 protein localization in any of our phosphomutant/mimetic cell lines compared with wild-type SRSF6 (predominantly nuclear in all cases) (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 6C

claim: Expression of SRSF6S303D decreases levels of Bax-κ transcripts compared with wild-type SRSF6-expressing macrophages
source: We observed that expression of SRSF6S303D decreased levels of Bax-κ transcripts, compared with those in wild-type SRSF6-expressing macrophages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: SRSF6S303D-expressing cell lines have higher levels of canonical Bax transcripts relative to wild-type SRSF6-expressing cells
source: Likewise, SRSF6S303D-expressing cell lines had higher levels of canonical Bax transcripts, relative to wild-type SRSF6-expressing cells, by semi-quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 6E

claim: Expression of the SRSF6S303D phosphomimetic allele renders cells less prone to apoptosis and cell death
source: Consistent with altered Bax-κ to Bax ratios in SRSF6S303D-expressing cell lines, expression of the SRSF6S303D phosphomimetic allele rendered cells less prone to apoptosis (annexin V+/PI-) and cell death (Figure 6F–H)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and cell death data in Figures 6F-H

claim: Phosphorylation of SRSF6 at S303 promotes splicing of Bax to generate the canonical BAX protein and limit apoptosis
source: Together, these data suggest that phosphorylation of SRSF6 at S303 promotes splicing of Bax, to generate the canonical BAX protein and limit apoptosis
evidence: Inferred from effects of SRSF6S303D on Bax splicing and cell death

claim: An approximately 2-fold decrease in Srsf6 transcript abundance is consistently detected at various time points following M. tuberculosis infection of macrophages
source: We consistently detected an approximately 2-fold decrease in Srsf6 transcript abundance at various time points following M. tuberculosis infection of macrophages, as well as in the lung homogenates collected from Mtb-infected mice (day 21 and 77 post-infection) (Figure 7A–B)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figures 7A-B

claim: Direct stimulation of dsDNA sensing via transfection leads to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
source: Direct stimulation of these pathways via transfection of dsDNA (Figure 7C) or treatment with recombinant IFN-β (rIFN-β) (Figure 7D) also led to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7C

claim: Treatment with recombinant IFN-β leads to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
source: Direct stimulation of these pathways via transfection of dsDNA (Figure 7C) or treatment with recombinant IFN-β (rIFN-β) (Figure 7D) also led to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7D

claim: Infection with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium leads to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
source: Direct stimulation of these pathways via transfection of dsDNA (Figure 7C) or treatment with recombinant IFN-β (rIFN-β) (Figure 7D) also led to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance, as did infection with the gram-negative bacterial pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Figure 7E)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7E

claim: Engagement of TLR-4 via LPS leads to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
source: Direct stimulation of these pathways via transfection of dsDNA (Figure 7C) or treatment with recombinant IFN-β (rIFN-β) (Figure 7D) also led to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance, as did infection with the gram-negative bacterial pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Figure 7E), engagement of TLR-4 via LPS (Figure 7F)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7F

claim: Infection with VSV leads to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance
source: Direct stimulation of these pathways via transfection of dsDNA (Figure 7C) or treatment with recombinant IFN-β (rIFN-β) (Figure 7D) also led to downregulation of Srsf6 transcript abundance, as did infection with the gram-negative bacterial pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Figure 7E), engagement of TLR-4 via LPS (Figure 7F) and infection with the RNA virus VSV (Figure 7G)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7G

claim: Downregulation of Srsf6 mRNA levels is part of the general macrophage pathogen sensing response
source: These data suggest that downregulation of Srsf6 mRNA levels is part of the general macrophage pathogen sensing response
evidence: Inferred from consistent downregulation across multiple pathogen types and immune stimuli

claim: Mtb grows significantly better in Srsf6 KD cell lines compared with SCR controls
source: Remarkably, we found that Mtb grew significantly better in Srsf6 KD cell lines compared with SCR controls (Figure 7H)
evidence: Supported by luciferase-based bacterial growth assay data in Figure 7H

claim: Increased Mtb replication in Srsf6 KD cells is concomitant with hyperinduction of Ifnb1 and interferon stimulated genes
source: This increase in Mtb replication was concomitant with hyperinduction of Ifnb1 and interferon stimulated genes, consistent with high basal type I IFN potentiating type I IFN responses (Figure 7I; West et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7I and citation to West et al., 2015

claim: More Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells stain PI+ compared with SCR controls over a 40+h Mtb infection
source: Along with harboring higher Mtb bacterial burdens, more Srsf6 KD RAW MΦ cells stained PI + compared with SCR controls over a 40+h Mtb infection (Figure 7J)
evidence: Supported by PI incorporation data during Mtb infection in Figure 7J

claim: SRSF6 plays a critical role in controlling inflammatory gene expression and cell death during bacterial infection
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate a critical role for SRSF6 in controlling inflammatory gene expression and cell death during bacterial infection
evidence: Inferred from multiple infection experiments showing altered gene expression and cell death

claim: Regulation of SRSF6 at post-translational and transcriptional levels constitutes an unappreciated layer of complexity in the macrophage innate immune response
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate a critical role for SRSF6 in controlling inflammatory gene expression and cell death during bacterial infection and suggest that regulation of SRSF6, both at the post-translational and transcriptional levels, constitutes an unappreciated layer of complexity in the macrophage innate immune response
evidence: Inferred from observations of SRSF6 phosphorylation and transcriptional regulation during infection

claim: SRSF6-dependent control of the ratio of BAX to BAX-κ isoforms balances critical aspects of innate immune homeostasis in macrophages
source: Here, we identify the splicing factor SRSF6 as a primary regulator of Bax pre-mRNA splicing in murine macrophages. We show that SRSF6-dependent control of the ratio of BAX to BAX-κ isoforms balances critical aspects of innate immune homeostasis in both macrophage-like cell lines and primary macrophages
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing effects of SRSF6 on Bax splicing and downstream phenotypes

claim: Expression of BAX-κ promotes upregulation of basal type I IFN expression driven by cytosolic mtDNA
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that expression of BAX-κ promotes upregulation of basal type I IFN expression driven by cytosolic mtDNA and renders cells prone to apoptotic cell death
evidence: Supported by BAX-κ overexpression experiments and mtDNA measurements

claim: Expression of BAX-κ renders cells prone to apoptotic cell death
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that expression of BAX-κ promotes upregulation of basal type I IFN expression driven by cytosolic mtDNA and renders cells prone to apoptotic cell death
evidence: Supported by cell death assays with BAX-κ overexpression

claim: BAX requires a signal to direct mitochondrial targeting and pore formation
source: Unlike BAX, which requires a signal to direct mitochondrial targeting and pore formation, BAX-κ is sufficient to trigger type I IFN expression and cell death in resting macrophages (Figure 5B–D)
evidence: Supported by comparison of BAX and BAX-κ overexpression experiments and established knowledge

claim: BAX-κ positions as a potential uncoupler of immunostimulatory mitochondrial DAMP release from cell death
source: These findings position BAX-κ as a potential uncoupler of immunostimulatory mitochondrial DAMP release from cell death and suggests that BAX-κ plays a role in promoting the primed antiviral state that innate immune cells, such as macrophages, must maintain
evidence: Inferred from observations that BAX-κ can release mtDNA and induce ISGs without full apoptosis

claim: Upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of breast cancer cells
source: Consistent with this, upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of breast cancer cells (Park et al., 2019), colorectal cancer cells (Wan et al., 2019), and lung cancer cells (Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2019, Wan et al., 2019, and Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013

claim: Upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of colorectal cancer cells
source: Consistent with this, upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of breast cancer cells (Park et al., 2019), colorectal cancer cells (Wan et al., 2019), and lung cancer cells (Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2019, Wan et al., 2019, and Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013

claim: Upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of lung cancer cells
source: Consistent with this, upregulation of SRSF6 promotes proliferation of breast cancer cells (Park et al., 2019), colorectal cancer cells (Wan et al., 2019), and lung cancer cells (Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2019, Wan et al., 2019, and Cohen-Eliav et al., 2013

claim: SRSF6 can promote expression of pro-apoptotic forms of proteins like BIM (BIM-S)
source: At the same time, SRSF6 can also promote expression of pro-apoptotic forms of proteins like BIM (BIM-S) (Hara et al., 2013) and cassette exon inclusion in the apoptotic factor FAS (Choi et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hara et al., 2013 and Choi et al., 2022

claim: SRSF6 can promote cassette exon inclusion in the apoptotic factor FAS
source: At the same time, SRSF6 can also promote expression of pro-apoptotic forms of proteins like BIM (BIM-S) (Hara et al., 2013) and cassette exon inclusion in the apoptotic factor FAS (Choi et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hara et al., 2013 and Choi et al., 2022

claim: Zn(2+)-dependent phosphorylation of SRSF6 has been associated with apoptosis via generation of BIM-S
source: Zn(2+)-dependent phosphorylation of SRSF6 has previously been associated with apoptosis via generation of BIM-S (Hara et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hara et al., 2013

claim: Ubiquitin-mediated control of SRSF6 protein levels has been linked to exon skipping in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
source: Zn(2+)-dependent phosphorylation of SRSF6 has previously been associated with apoptosis via generation of BIM-S (Hara et al., 2013) and ubiquitin-mediated control of SRSF6 protein levels has been linked to exon skipping in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Zhou et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2020

claim: Apoptotic caspases suppress cGAS-dependent type I IFN expression via mtDNA released by BAX/BAK pores during mitochondrial apoptosis
source: Seminal work from White et al. and Rongveux et al. implicates apoptotic caspases in suppressing cGAS-dependent type I IFN expression via mtDNA released by BAX/BAK pores during mitochondrial apoptosis (Rongvaux et al., 2014; White et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rongvaux et al., 2014 and White et al., 2014

claim: BAX/BAK release of mtDNA and apoptotic cell death can be uncoupled
source: However, our work and that of others, begin to suggest that BAX/BAK release of mtDNA and apoptotic cell death can in fact be uncoupled (Riley et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by current work and citation to Riley et al., 2018

claim: Large BAX/BAK 'macropores' that form at late stages of apoptosis allow herniation and extrusion of the inner membrane, releasing mtDNA from the matrix
source: Large BAX/BAK 'macropores' that form at late stages of apoptosis have been shown to allow herniation and extrusion of the inner membrane, releasing mtDNA from the matrix (McArthur et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2018

claim: BAK pores are more immunogenic than BAX pores and enable faster mtDNA release
source: Specifically, BAK pores are more immunogenic than BAX pores and enable faster mtDNA release (Cosentino et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cosentino et al., 2022

claim: Cell death modality usage is a critical factor in determining Mtb pathogenesis
source: Numerous reports demonstrate that cell death modality usage is a critical factor in determining Mtb pathogenesis
evidence: Supported by general knowledge in the field

claim: Apoptosis controls Mtb replication and spread while necrotic cell death promotes it
source: The established paradigm in the Mtb field asserts that apoptosis controls Mtb replication and spread while necrotic cell death promotes it (Abarca-Rojano et al., 2003; Abebe et al., 2011; Aguilo et al., 2013; Aguiló et al., 2014; Behar et al., 2010; Behar et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Abarca-Rojano et al., 2003; Abebe et al., 2011; Aguilo et al., 2013; Aguiló et al., 2014; Behar et al., 2010; Behar et al., 2011
